newsitem.title: USA: Aluminum can market share to fall in U.S./Europe.
newsitem.headline: Aluminum can market share to fall in U.S./Europe.

text.p: The aluminum beverage can's share of the soft drinks and beer packaging markets in Europe and the U.S. were headed for a further fall this year, with poor prospects for any strong growth in the future, said Nick Mason, analyst with CRU International Ltd.

In the U.S. the beverage can's share of packaged soft drink and beer has fallen from 58 percent in 1994 to 54 percent last year, and the decline reflected growing popularity of PET plastic bottles for soft drinks and glass bottles for premium beer, Mason said.
"We expect cans to lose another 1 percent share this year," Mason said referring to the U.S. market.
Mason was speaking to delegates at the Aluminum Association's Alumitech 97 conference.
Almost all beverage cans in the U.S. are made from aluminum, one of the biggest markets in the world for the metal. In Europe steel is a big rival to aluminum cans.
In Europe, CRU estimated that the can's share was just over 15 percemt of beer and soft drinks packaging, and expected that share to fall below this level in 1997.
He expressed surprise by the swiftness with which the can seems to have stalled in Europe and attributed this to transfer of PET technology from the U.S. to plants overseas.
In terms of can production, Mason expected U.S. can production to fall this year to 100.8 billion units from 102.1 billion units last year.
In Europe he expects production to rise slightly because of last year's cold summer and sees production this year at 30.6 billion units compared with 29.6 billion last year.
But Mason also expected aluminum's share of the European can market to slip below 50 percent.

"PET is looking more competitive than ever before," Mason said. Aluminum prices were expected to firm this year to an average $1,630 per tonne, in the meantime the cost of PET resins are expected to slump to an average of $1,100 per tonne.
He had already reports of resin prices well below this level.
"The evidence suggests that in the USA and Europe, the aluminum can is entering its middle years," Mason said. "Any extra growth is going to be extremely hard won and probably marginal in volume."
Mason said the can market in the U.S. seems to have moved from maturity phase to saturation. Europe was lagging the U.S. in this same transition by three to four years.

Mason warned that aluminum cans could see a nightmare situation of the type that plagued aluminum windows in the U.S. in the last decade when prices peaked in early 1980s and then entered uninterrupted period of decline beginning 1985.
Over that time period aluminum windows saw market share fall from above 55 percent to below 20 percent while the market share for vinyl grew from virtually nothing to one third of the market in 1996.
